key_terms.meaning: A 4-tuple (N, Σ, R, S): nonterminals N, terminals Σ, rewrite rules A → β with A in N, and a start symbol S in N.
Terminals are the actual words (dog, the); nonterminals are phrase labels (S, NP, VP) that stand for groups of words.
The single nonterminal every derivation begins from, usually S for sentence.
A step-by-step rewriting from S to a string of terminals, each step replacing one nonterminal by the right side of a rule.
A derivation that always rewrites the leftmost nonterminal first; it gives one canonical order per parse tree.
A tree whose root is S, internal nodes are rule applications, and leaves are the words in order.
The string of leaf labels read left to right; the sentence the tree derives.
Generation runs rules forward from S to make strings; recognition decides whether a given string has a derivation from S.
A set of attribute–value pairs, e.g. [NUM sg, PERS 3], attached to a node to carry agreement and subcategorisation.
Merging two feature structures; it succeeds only if shared attributes have compatible values and fails on a clash such as sg vs pl.
A corpus of sentences that humans have annotated with full parse trees, used to train and test parsers.
A CFG where every rule is A → B C or A → w; only the start symbol may derive the empty string ε.
A bottom-up parser for CNF grammars that fills a table cell[i,j] with all nonterminals spanning words i..j; time O(n³·|G|).
A top-down chart parser that reads words left to right and stores dotted rules A → α • β, so partial parses are shared, not re-searched.
When a phrase such as a prepositional phrase can hang from more than one node, giving several parse trees for one string.
A CFG with a probability on every rule, summing to 1 per left-hand side; a tree's probability is the product of its rule probabilities.
A description of a sentence as words linked by head → dependent arcs with grammatical labels, with no phrasal nodes.
A flat, non-overlapping group of words such as a noun group, marked without internal structure.
A PCFG whose nonterminals carry their head word, e.g. VP(saw), so rule probabilities depend on which words are involved.
A left-to-right parser with a stack and a queue of remaining words; it either shifts a word onto the stack or reduces top stack items by a rule.

takeaways: A context-free grammar is a handful of rewrite rules that can generate infinitely many sentences, and English phrase structure fits this form well.
Generation goes from S to a sentence; recognition goes from a sentence back to trees, and parsing is recognition plus building the trees.
Chomsky normal form turns any CFG into binary rules, which is exactly the shape the CYK table needs.
CYK and Earley both avoid blind search: CYK fills spans bottom-up, Earley shares partial parses across the whole sentence.
A grammar alone cannot pick between parses; ambiguity is resolved with probabilities, head words, or meaning.
A PCFG scores every tree as a product of rule probabilities, so the best tree is found by dynamic programming rather than enumeration.
Dependency grammar drops phrases and links words directly, which suits free word order languages and gives fast linear-time parsers.
Shallow parsing gives flat chunks cheaply and is often enough for named entities or noun-group extraction.
Lexicalizing a PCFG with head words fixes many wrong attachments that a plain PCFG prefers.
Shift-reduce parsing builds trees with a stack and a queue and runs in time linear in sentence length.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine definitions with worked traces: a derivation or parse tree, a filled CYK or Earley table, a probability calculation, and a discussion of ambiguity and its resolution.

bank.q: Define a context-free grammar as a 4-tuple and write a small grammar for English that covers a determiner–noun subject, a transitive verb, and a prepositional phrase. Give a leftmost derivation and the parse tree for one sentence, and name its yield.
outline: Correct 4-tuple with N, Σ, R, S and each component explained
Rules for S, NP, VP, PP, Det, N, V, P with lexical rules
Leftmost derivation shown step by step
Matching parse tree with S at the root and words at leaves
Yield stated as the sentence string

bank.q: Explain the difference between generation and recognition. Why does a grammar that generates a sentence also serve as a recogniser, and what extra work does a parser do beyond recognition?
outline: Generation: rules applied forward from S to produce strings
Recognition: given a string, decide whether S derives it
Grammar defines the same relation read in either direction
Parser also builds and returns the tree or trees, and may rank them
Mention infinite language from finite rules

bank.q: Why is a plain context-free grammar not enough for English agreement? Explain feature structures and unification, and show a unification that succeeds and one that fails.
outline: Example: 'the dogs barks' is licensed by an agreement-blind CFG
Feature structure as attribute–value pairs such as NUM, PERS
Unification merges structures and fails on conflicting values
Worked success: [NUM sg] with [PERS 3] giving both
Worked failure: [NUM sg] with [NUM pl]
Rules carry features up from head to phrase

bank.q: What is a treebank? Describe how treebank trees are produced and how they are used in building a parser, and state two difficulties with treebank annotation.
outline: Definition: corpus with human-annotated full trees
Annotation by trained annotators with guidelines and checks
Uses: training a PCFG or statistical parser, testing, grammar extraction
Difficulties: annotator disagreement, flat or inconsistent structures, cost

bank.q: Define Chomsky normal form and explain why parsers want it. Convert the rules S → NP VP PP and PP → P NP into CNF, introducing new nonterminals where needed.
outline: CNF: only A → B C and A → w; ε allowed only from start symbol
Reason: binary branching fixes the split points CYK needs
S → NP VP PP becomes S → X PP, X → NP VP
PP → P NP becomes PP → P NP (already binary) or introduce a terminal rule
Show any ternary rule is binarised by new nonterminals

bank.q: Using a CNF grammar given in the question, run the CYK algorithm on a five-word sentence and fill the table cell by cell. State the complexity and say how the table proves the sentence is or is not in the language.
outline: Diagonal cells from lexical rules
Fill by span length, splitting each span at every internal position
Combine left and right nonterminals with binary rules
Correct final answer: S in cell[1,n] means accepted
Complexity O(n³·|G|) with n words and |G| grammar size
Empty top cell means no parse

bank.q: Trace the Earley parser on a short sentence with a small grammar. Show the chart entries as dotted rules with their origins, and explain the predictor, scanner and completer steps.
outline: Dotted rule A → α • β with start position
Initialisation with S → • γ at position 0
Predictor adds rules for the nonterminal after the dot
Scanner matches a terminal against the next word
Completer combines a finished rule with the rules waiting for it
Chart shows shared partial parses; final state S → γ • proves a parse

bank.q: A sentence contains a verb, an object noun phrase and a following prepositional phrase. Show at least two parse trees, name the ambiguity type, and describe three sources of evidence that can pick the right one.
outline: Two trees: PP attaches to the verb phrase or to the object noun phrase
This is attachment (structural) ambiguity, distinct from word-sense ambiguity
Evidence: lexical preference of the verb for a PP
Evidence: probabilities from a treebank-trained PCFG
Evidence: meaning and context, selectional preferences
Note number of parses grows fast with sentence length

bank.q: Given a PCFG with rule probabilities, compute the probability of a stated sentence under two different parse trees. Explain how the inside (Viterbi) algorithm finds the single most probable tree without listing all trees.
outline: Tree probability = product of rule probabilities used in the tree
Worked product with numbers, showing each rule's probability
Second tree computed and compared
Inside algorithm: for each span and nonterminal keep the best score
Recurrence over splits and binary rules, max instead of sum for Viterbi
Complexity O(n³·|G|) same as CYK

bank.q: Draw the dependency tree for a given sentence, labelling the arcs with subject, object, modifier and determiner relations. Then describe one transition-based parsing step sequence using shift and left-arc/right-arc actions.
outline: One head per word except the root, arcs do not cross
Correct attachment of subject to verb, object to verb, determiners to nouns
Labels drawn from a dependency scheme
Shift-reduce transitions with stack, buffer and arc set
Accepts a sentence in time linear in length for greedy parsers

bank.q: Convert a chunked sentence into IOB tags, then into BILOU tags. Explain the difference between labelled and unlabelled chunking and how chunk precision and recall are computed.
outline: B-X opens a chunk of type X, I-X continues it, O is outside
BILOU marks begin, inside, last, unit and outside
Labelled chunking gives the type; unlabelled only the boundary
Precision = correct chunks / predicted chunks; recall = correct / true chunks
F1 as harmonic mean

bank.q: Show the stack and the queue at every step of a shift-reduce parse of a short sentence under stated grammar rules. State the time complexity and one weakness of greedy shift-reduce parsing.
outline: Start with empty stack and full queue
Shift moves the front word to the stack
Reduce applies a binary rule to the top two items, pushing the new nonterminal
Correct final stack holding S with empty queue
Time O(n) with n words
Weakness: an early wrong decision cannot be undone in the greedy version

bank.q: Compare CYK, Earley and shift-reduce parsing on grammar form required, complexity in the general and unambiguous cases, and the ability to return all parses. Recommend one for a task that needs every parse of short sentences and justify the choice.
outline: CYK needs CNF, O(n³·|G|), returns all parses in the table
Earley works on any CFG, O(n³) general, O(n²) unambiguous, O(n) for bounded-state grammars
Shift-reduce is O(n) but usually returns one tree
CYK and Earley share work; no exponential blow-up
Recommendation justified by grammar form and need for all parses

bank.q: Explain why a plain PCFG makes poor attachment decisions, and how lexicalizing the grammar with head words and their subcategorisation fixes this. Illustrate with a verb that takes a prepositional phrase and one that does not.
outline: Plain PCFG conditions only on the nonterminal, so it cannot see the verb
Structural bias: prefers whichever attachment the treebank made more frequent
Lexicalized rule VP(verb) → VBD(verb) PP records the verb's own preference
Head word propagated up the tree
Example where a verb subcategorises for PP versus one where it does not
Sparsity problem and smoothing or back-off to unlexicalized rules

bank.q: Describe a full pipeline from a raw sentence to a parse tree using a treebank, a normal form, a parsing algorithm and probability estimation. Evaluate where the pipeline is likely to fail and how the errors can be measured.
outline: Tokenise and tag the sentence first
Extract a CFG from the treebank and binarise to CNF
Estimate rule probabilities from treebank counts with smoothing
Parse with probabilistic CYK, returning the best tree
Failures: unseen words, long sentences, annotation inconsistency, ambiguity
Evaluation by labelled bracket F1 or dependency attachment score

glossary.def: A finite set of rewrite rules whose left side is a single nonterminal, able to generate an infinite language.
A symbol that appears as a word in the sentence and is never rewritten.
A symbol such as NP or VP standing for a phrase and always rewritten by a rule.
The nonterminal from which every derivation begins, normally S.
A sequence of rule applications turning the start symbol into a sentence.
A tree recording which rule applied at each node, with words as leaves.
The left-to-right sequence of leaf labels of a parse tree.
A rule whose expansion contains its own nonterminal, which lets a grammar build unboundedly long sentences.
Producing strings by applying rules forward from the start symbol.
Deciding whether a given string can be derived from the start symbol.
A set of attribute–value pairs attached to a node to record number, person, case or subcategorisation.
Combining two feature structures, succeeding only when shared attributes agree.
A corpus of sentences annotated with full syntactic trees.
A grammar whose rules are only A → B C or A → w, with ε allowed only from the start symbol.
A bottom-up table parser for CNF grammars that fills spans by increasing length.
A chart parser that stores dotted rules with their start positions and reads the sentence left to right.
A grammar rule with a dot showing how much of its right side has been matched.
The property that one word string has more than one parse tree under a grammar.
Ambiguity over which node a phrase, typically a prepositional phrase, attaches to.
A CFG in which each rule carries a probability, so each tree gets a probability.
Dynamic programming that sums or maximises rule probabilities over every span and nonterminal.
A tree of words in which every word except the root has exactly one head.
A flat, non-overlapping group of words such as a noun group, marked without internal structure.
A tagging scheme using B-X, I-X and O to mark chunk boundaries and types.
A PCFG whose nonterminals include the head word, making rule probabilities word-sensitive.
A parser that uses a stack and a queue and applies shift or reduce actions in sequence.
